title: What can a vaginal bulge or heaviness mean? Understanding prolapse
seoTitle: Vaginal bulge or heaviness and prolapse signs
description: Heaviness or a vaginal bulge can signal pelvic organ prolapse. See NHS symptom lists, medical assessment, and where physiotherapy may fit without self-grading.
primaryQuestion: What are the symptoms of pelvic organ prolapse?
directAnswer: Pelvic organ prolapse is when the womb, bladder or bowel bulges into the vagina because pelvic support is reduced. The NHS lists possible symptoms as heaviness, discomfort or pressure in the lower tummy or vagina; feeling or seeing a bulge; pain, discomfort or numbness during sex; constipation or bowel difficulty; and bladder problems such as incomplete emptying, frequency or small leaks with cough, sneeze or exercise. Similar sensations can have other causes, so an examination, not an internet photo, decides what is going on.

sections.heading: Symptoms worth getting checked
paragraphs: See a doctor if you notice a lump in or around the vagina or any other symptoms from the NHS prolapse list above. Some prolapses are found during cervical screening or another exam when you felt little day-to-day change. Severity of bother does not always match what a photo on social media claims to show.

Track when heaviness is worse (end of day, after standing, during exercise) and whether bladder or bowel emptying changes. Our guide to pelvic-floor assessment symptoms explains why “weakness” alone is an incomplete label for these feelings.

sections.heading: What medical assessment usually involves
paragraphs: NHS advice: a GP asks about symptoms and examines you, which means undressing from the waist down. You may request a chaperone and, where available, a female doctor. Examination may be lying on your side or standing; a speculum may be used to look for prolapse. Grading may use a number from 1 to 4 in NHS explanations of severity.

NICE NG123 recommends a history covering prolapse, urinary, bowel and sexual function, examination to rule out a pelvic mass or other pathology, and, for specialist evaluation, recording compartment findings, often with the POP-Q system. Imaging is not routinely required to document a prolapse already found on examination. Repeat examination standing or squatting may be considered if symptoms and lying findings disagree.

sections.heading: Care options clinicians may discuss
paragraphs: NHS treatment choices depend on which organs are involved, how severe the prolapse is, your age, general health and whether you plan pregnancies. If symptoms are absent or not bothersome, monitoring without active treatment can be appropriate. Options that may be discussed include local hormone treatment categories, vaginal support pessaries, physiotherapy with pelvic-floor muscle training, and surgery for more severe or limiting cases.

NICE NG123 asks clinicians to discuss no treatment, non-surgical treatment and surgical options together with the woman. NICE also considers a supervised pelvic-floor muscle training programme of at least 16 weeks as a first option for symptomatic POP-Q stage 1 or 2 prolapse, advising continuation if beneficial. Pessaries and surgery are medical decisions, not something a physiotherapy article can select for you.

sections.heading: Where pelvic health physiotherapy can fit
paragraphs: NICE NG210 suggests considering supervised pelvic-floor muscle training for at least four months for women with symptomatic prolapse that does not extend more than 1 cm beyond the hymen on straining. NHS self-help points include avoiding heavy strain where advised, managing constipation, and regular pelvic-floor exercises once technique is suitable. Training still needs contraction and relaxation assessment; squeezing through pain is not the plan.

Dr. Zalak Shah (PT) can help with symptom strategies, pressure management for daily tasks and supervised programmes. She does not diagnose prolapse stage as a substitute for medical examination, and she does not promise that exercise reverses every prolapse.

sections.heading: Activity worries and personal goals
paragraphs: NHS guidance advises avoiding activities that put a lot of strain on the pelvic floor, such as heavy lifting, running and trampolining, while you work with clinicians on a plan. That does not mean permanent inactivity for everyone. Goals such as walking, returning to a modified class, or managing childcare lifts should be stated clearly so advice matches your life.

Seek urgent medical care for inability to pass urine, severe uncontrolled pain, or a bulge you cannot reduce with advice you have already been given by your clinician. New heavy bleeding or fever with pelvic pain also needs prompt medical review rather than waiting for a routine physio slot.

faqs.question: Can I tell the stage of prolapse from a mirror check at home?
faqs.answer: No. Staging systems such as POP-Q are clinical tools used during examination. Home looking can increase anxiety without giving a reliable grade and should not replace medical assessment.

faqs.question: If I have no symptoms, do I still need treatment?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. The NHS notes that if you have no symptoms or the prolapse is not bothering you, you may not need medical treatment. Decisions still belong with your clinician after examination.
